[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: 'multiply two tables' suggests multiplying matching entries (as addition adds them), and ordinary multiplication commutes. Rule: each product entry c[i][j] is the dot product of row i of a and column j of b, and AB generally differs from BA.
[1] misconception (M) -> MatrixProductIsElementwise: wrong rule: c[i][j] = a[i][j] * b[i][j] computes the matrix product. Right rule: c[i][j] is the dot product of row i of a with column j of b: the sum over k of a[i][k]*b[k][j].
[2] misconception (M) -> MatrixProductCommutes: wrong rule: A * B and B * A are the same matrix. Right rule: Matrix multiplication is not commutative; changing the order may change the product, and for non-square matrices one order may not even be defined.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> MatrixProductIsElementwise: Points to LT: the innermost k loop finishes accumulating c[i][j] before j moves on. Inconsistent application: c[i][j] is reset inside the k loop on some passes, or a[k][i] is used instead of a[i][k]. (here mixing in: "c[i][j] = a[i][j] * b[i][j] computes the matrix product")
[4] misconception (M) -> WholeArrayArithmetic: wrong rule: a = a + b adds the arrays element by element. Right rule: Java has no arithmetic on whole arrays; write nested loops that compute c[i][j] = a[i][j] + b[i][j].
[5] misconception (M) -> ColumnLikeRow: wrong rule: Column j of a 2-D array can be picked out as a 1-D array, just like row a[i]. Right rule: There is no column expression; the product reads column j of b element by element as b[k][j] in the k loop.

[0] names_the_element (N): Identity: matrix addition and multiplication implemented with nested for loops over 2-D arrays.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Declarative: sum c[i][j] = a[i][j] + b[i][j]; product c[i][j] = sum over k of a[i][k]*b[k][j]; the product is defined only when the columns of a equal the rows of b.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Sequencing: create c (all 0.0); for each i, for each j, for k = 0..N-1 add a[i][k]*b[k][j] into c[i][j]. The k loop completes for each (i, j) before j increases.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Result: a new N-by-N double matrix c. In the book's example c[1][2] = .3*.5 + .6*.1 + .1*.4 = .25.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): State transition: one innermost step adds one product a[i][k]*b[k][j] to c[i][j]; nothing else changes.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Matrices are stored as 2-D arrays and read entry by entry as a[i][j].
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Addition uses two nested loops (i, j); multiplication adds a third inner loop over k for each dot product.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): The power method repeats vector-matrix multiplication rather than matrix-matrix multiplication, because that is all it needs.
[3] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan/role: c[i][j] is a gatherer (running sum) for one dot product. The whole computation implements linear-algebra operations used throughout science and engineering.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> MatrixProductIsElementwise: Conservation: reordering the i, j, k loops keeps the product (only the summation order changes); swapping a and b changes it. Reusing a c that is not zeroed adds the old values in.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Applicability: use nested-loop matrix code for small and moderate matrices. When only a vector times a matrix is needed (power method), use vector-matrix multiplication, which is far cheaper than matrix-matrix.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The product sums a[i][k]*b[k][j] over k. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: the element-wise c[i][j] = a[i][j]*b[i][j] is used for the product
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Columns of a must equal rows of b. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: non-square matrices with mismatched inner dimensions, or loop bounds swapped (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Arrays have no arithmetic operators. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: c = a + b or a * b written for 2-D arrays (bad operand types)

The power method is repeated vector-matrix multiplication.
Matrix addition uses two nested loops over i and j, and matrix multiplication adds a third inner loop over k to compute each dot product c[i][j].
Matrix operations index a[i][j] in nested loops.
